title.rendered: V Foundation grants power colorectal cancer research

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Kayla McMahon

The V Foundation for Cancer Research once again demonstrated its remarkable generosity and commitment to advancing cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute by awarding $1.4 million in grants to two exceptional investigators. Grant recipients Edward Chouchani, PhD, and Gabriel Griffin, MD, are leading projects that are pivotal in enhancing the understanding and treatment of colorectal cancers, the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States, because of the invaluable support of the V Foundation.

Chouchani’s research is supported by the V Foundation’s Adult Translational Grant, which focuses on moving novel strategies from the laboratory to human clinical trials. He investigates how cancer cells manipulate nutrient usage to grow and spread, particularly through enzymes called creatine kinases (CKs). These enzymes are crucial for the growth and sustenance of colon cancer cells but not for healthy ones, presenting a unique target for treatment. Chouchani developed a promising new medicine that inhibits CKs, effectively killing cancer cells reliant on these enzymes. His next step is to test this medicine in animal models, a critical precursor to human trials.

“We are grateful for their dedication to accelerating victory over cancer® and saving lives.”

Kara Coleman, PhD, V Foundation for Cancer Research

Griffin’s research is funded by the V Foundation’s V Scholar Grant, which supports early career, tenure-track faculty in their laboratory-based or translational research endeavors. He aims to enhance immunotherapy by understanding how cancer cells evade the immune system. Griffin’s lab investigates ancient viruses embedded in human DNA, typically silenced by epigenetic repressors. By activating these viruses in cancer cells, Griffin hopes to stimulate the immune system to target and destroy tumors, potentially paving the way for new cancer therapies, especially for patients unresponsive to existing immunotherapies.

Kara Coleman, PhD, Vice President of Grants and Research at the V Foundation, expressed her enthusiasm for the recipients. “We are proud to fund the best and brightest scientists in the cancer research space and are thrilled to congratulate Drs. Ed Chouchani and Gabe Griffin as V Foundation grantees,” she shared. “We are grateful for their dedication to accelerating Victory Over Cancer® and saving lives.”

The V Foundation’s generosity is crucial in helping Dana-Farber sustain its momentum of research and discovery. Through their support, investigators like Chouchani and Griffin are translating groundbreaking research into new treatment options, which is improving outcomes and offering hope to cancer patients worldwide. By investing in pioneering scientists, the V Foundation is ensuring that innovative therapies reach patients’ bedsides and helping to create a future where all cancers are treatable.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Prostate Cancer Foundation fuels Dana-Farber innovation with $1M+ in grants
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: PCF recently awarded $1,050,000 to three Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers through two Young Investigator Awards and one Challenge Award, each supporting research projects aimed at combating prostate cancer and improving outcomes for patients.

jetpack-related-posts.title: IWMF awards $1.4 million to Dana-Farber investigators, fueling Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: For more than two decades, the International Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia Foundation (IWMF) has been a vital philanthropic partner to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, accelerating research into Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinemia (WM), a rare, slow-growing blood cancer.

jetpack-related-posts.title: CRI grants accelerate immunotherapy research at Dana-Farber
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Cancer Research Institute (CRI) is advancing bold new strategies to harness the immune system against cancer through two grants at DanaFarber Cancer Institute.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Damon Runyon supports bold research by emerging talent
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation has awarded $1.22 million in grants to four early career investigators at Dana-Farber whose research has the potential to yield important breakthroughs in cancer prevention, diagnosis, and treatment.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Susan G. Komen strengthens commitment to breast cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: In 2024, Komen reaffirmed its dedication to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute by awarding three new Career Transition Awards totaling $1.95 million, alongside 12 active research grants. This investment underscores Komen's ongoing support for groundbreaking studies and improving outcomes for those affected by breast cancer.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation invests in tomorrow’s discoveries
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Dana-Farber received over $3,156,000 in grants from the Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation in 2024 supporting 10 physician-scientists and researchers.

title.rendered: Basic research is focus of Mathers Charitable Foundation grants

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Kathy Clute
Photography by Sam Ogden

The G. Harold and Leila Y. Mathers Charitable Foundation has awarded Dana-Farber $1.47 million to support two Institute researchers investigating how cancer develops and how cells detect and respond to viral infections.

“We believe that transformative breakthroughs in cancer will come from a thorough understanding of the fundamental mechanisms by which it arises and grows,” said Zach Handelman, vice president and treasurer of the Mathers Foundation. “We feel privileged to fund this work at Dana-Farber and look forward to the new knowledge it will generate.”

Since 1991, the foundation has invested more than $17 million in basic and translational research at the Institute. The 2024 grants were awarded to microbiologist Philip Kranzusch, PhD, and pediatric oncologist David Pellman, MD, Margaret M. Dyson Professorship in Pediatric Oncology at Harvard Medical School.

Kranzusch’s team is investigating how cells respond to viral pathogens and how those signaling pathways can be harnessed to create potential new therapies for cancer and autoimmune diseases. “Human cells have a set of protein sensors that detect viral infections and quickly trigger immune responses,” said Kranzusch. “Interestingly, key components of antiviral immunity evolved billions of years ago in bacteria as mechanisms to defend against viruses called phages.”

The lab aims to understand how two bacterial defense systems work together to prevent phages from reproducing, possibly by forming complex structures that degrade viral DNA. The research team has discovered human immune genes with structural similarities, which may enable them to identify previously unknown proteins that play a role in the human immune response to viral infections.

Pellman and his colleagues study cell division and chromosome segregation errors in cancer and the impact of these faults on cancer genome structure. Nuclear atypia—unusual changes in the size and shape of cell nuclei—are a common feature of many tumors and have been used since the 1920s to assess tumor severity and predict outcomes. Previous research funded by the Mathers Foundation has found that these nuclear changes significantly affect genome rearrangements in human cancers.

It is possible that DNA changes and shifts in gene expression in atypical nuclei might be influenced by the formation of nuclear bodies around chromosomes after cells divide. Pellman is using advanced single-cell genomic technologies developed in his lab to zero in on specific nuclear bodies known as MN/53BP1, which are part of the cell’s response to DNA damage. A better understanding of how cells respond to DNA damage could lead to improved cancer treatments.

jetpack-related-posts.title: High-risk, high-reward research is The Mathers Foundation’s priority
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Transformative basic research is the focus of The G. Harold and Leila Y. Mathers Charitable Foundation, which recently awarded $1.5 million to fund Dana-Farber research on unraveling the inner workings of human cells.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Mathers Foundation grants promote basic cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Many of today’s important advances in cancer care trace their origins to basic research—a form of scientific investigation aimed at uncovering the fundamental principles of biology, chemistry, and foundational science.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Pew Charitable Trusts
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Pew Charitable Trusts provided $430,000 in support of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers Evanna Mills, PhD, and Brenda Nakagaki, PhD. The investment will fuel investigations into how metabolic dysfunction impacts immune cell function, particularly macrophages, and triggers harmful inflammation in different cells and tissues.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation gift focuses on cancer interception
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: A $1.25 million gift to Dana-Farber from the Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation supports research focused on ways pancreatic cancer might be detected—and intercepted—before it can be seen on CT scans or other imaging modalities.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Prostate Cancer Foundation fuels Dana-Farber innovation with $1M+ in grants
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: PCF recently awarded $1,050,000 to three Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers through two Young Investigator Awards and one Challenge Award, each supporting research projects aimed at combating prostate cancer and improving outcomes for patients.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Carney family remains steadfast in support of breast cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: With a recent $1 million gift, the Carney Family Charitable Foundation, led by Trustees Patrick and Lillian Carney, has expanded a legacy of support for breast cancer immuno-oncology research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute that spans over 20 years.

title.rendered: Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation gift focuses on cancer interception

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Kathy Clute
Photography by Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation

Cancer of the pancreas is a leading cause of cancer death because it is usually not discovered until it has progressed to a late stage, when treatment options are limited. A $1.25 million gift to Dana-Farber from the Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation seeks to change that by supporting research focused on ways the disease might be detected—and intercepted—before it can be seen on CT scans or other imaging modalities.

Ilene Beal was a pioneering banking executive from Wellesley, Mass., who generously mentored other women in business for years before her death from cancer in 2015. She is remembered as a warm, caring person who was always thinking of others and ready to help. For nearly 10 years, Beal was treated by Jeffrey Wisch, MD, who was a senior physician at Dana-Farber.

The Beal Foundation’s 2025 gift of $1.25 million establishes the Ilene Beal Fund to Eradicate Cancer and builds on past gifts, including to the Ilene Beal & Jeffrey S. Wisch, MD, Clinical Investigator Fund.

The latest gift will support research led by Brian Wolpin, MD, MPH, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Center and the Robert T. and Judith B. Hale Chair in Pancreatic Cancer at Dana-Farber. Wolpin is testing the ability of small molecule inhibitors to target mutations in the KRAS oncogene found in precursor lesions called pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN). These lesions cannot be detected using current imaging techniques, and more than 90 percent of pancreatic cancers have KRAS gene mutations.

KRAS inhibitors have shown promise in patients with advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas, and Wolpin, who is also director, Hale Family Center for Pancreatic Cancer Research, intends to use those molecules to develop new imaging methods and interception strategies. This will permit oncologists to identify high-risk PanINs and treat them before they have a chance to become invasive cancers. For example, radiolabeled versions of the inhibitors could be used with PET imaging to find lesions that cannot now be detected, allowing them to be non-invasively monitored over time.

In 2025, 67,440 Americans are expected to be diagnosed with pancreatic cancer and an estimated 51,980 people may die from it, according to the National Cancer Institute.

“Ilene was a mentor, a role model, a collaborative and talented executive who worked hard at everything she did, because she believed that with dedication and focused work one could accomplish anything,” said Brian Potts, a trustee of the Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation. “She would be thrilled to fund this pathbreaking research because she knew firsthand the challenges of cancer.”

excerpt.rendered: A $1.25 million gift to Dana-Farber from the Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation supports research focused on ways pancreatic cancer might be detected—and intercepted—before it can be seen on CT scans or other imaging modalities.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Gift continues donor’s legacy by supporting gastrointestinal research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Throughout her life, Ilene Beal was dedicated to hard work and breaking down barriers. She became a female pioneer in the Boston banking world and was a valued mentor for other women in the industry.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Carney family remains steadfast in support of breast cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: With a recent $1 million gift, the Carney Family Charitable Foundation, led by Trustees Patrick and Lillian Carney, has expanded a legacy of support for breast cancer immuno-oncology research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute that spans over 20 years.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Crystal Family Charitable Foundation
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Crystal Family Charitable Foundation recently made a generous $200,000 gift to support a variety of research and patient care programs at Dana-Farber. The funds will drive innovative prostate and pancreatic cancer research while enhancing social services offered to pediatric patients and grieving families.

img.alt_text: Three people pose for a photo in front of mountains

jetpack-related-posts.title: Sally Naser Charitable Foundation
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Sally Naser Charitable Foundation, led by Camille and Robert Naser, made a $200,000 gift in support of early career investigators whose research drives breakthroughs, improves patient outcomes, and advances pediatric sarcoma care and research. This gift builds upon many years of support in honor of their daughter, Sally.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Basic research is focus of Mathers Charitable Foundation grants
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The G. Harold and Leila Y. Mathers Charitable Foundation has awarded Dana-Farber $1.47 million to support two Institute researchers investigating how cancer develops and how cells detect and respond to viral infections.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The National Breast Cancer Foundation
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The National Breast Cancer Foundation has made a generous gift of $170,000 to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute as part of their ongoing support. This latest gift plays a crucial role in advancing our mission to defy cancer and enhance breast cancer patient outcomes.

title.rendered: IWMF awards over $1.1 million to Dana-Farber for WM research advancements

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Cyrena Musset

The International Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia Foundation (IWMF) has taken a significant step forward in combating Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinemia (WM) by awarding four Dana-Farber scientists more than $1.1 million in grants. This generous funding is intended to fuel groundbreaking studies that aim to uncover the mechanisms behind WM development, pinpoint vulnerabilities, and identify novel drug targets.

WM is a rare, slow-growing form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that typically forms in bone marrow. While it can be treated, the disease remains incurable and treatment resistant. Additionally, given its rarity, testing new therapies can be difficult due to the relatively small patient population. The generosity of IWMF will support the work of these Dana-Farber researchers in advancing scientific breakthroughs in WM.

Yoshinobu “Yoshi” Konishi, PhD, is an instructor in the Ghobrial Lab at Dana-Farber and a recipient of the Robert A. Kyle Career Development Award from IWMF. His research focuses on clarifying cell-cell interactions within the bone marrow microenvironment of patients with plasma cell malignancies with a special focus on early precursor stages. Konishi’s work is essential to understanding how these interactions contribute to the progression of WM and other related diseases.

Filip Garbicz, MD, is a researcher and postdoctoral research fellow at Dana-Farber’s Carrasco Lab in the Department of Pathology and is also a recipient of the Robert A. Kyle Career Development Award. He is focused on studying cancer cell-intrinsic and microenvironmental roles of MYD88 mutations and chromosome 6q deletion in mature B-cell malignancies, with special focus on WM.

His research aims to unravel the genetic complexities that drive WM, potentially leading to targeted therapies that address these specific mutations.

Maria Luisa Guerrera, MD, is a hematologist in Dana-Farber’s Division of Hematologic Neoplasia. She is studying the genomic events that are responsible for WM disease progression following the acquisition of the MYD88 mutation and investigating ways to halt or reverse WM advancement.

“We are excited to support Dana-Farber’s innovative research and pave the way for new treatment strategies and better outcomes for patients.”

Paul Kitchen, The International Waldenström’s Macroglobulinemia Foundation

Zachary Hunter, PhD, is the Bliss Family Investigator at the Bing Center for Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia where he oversees genomic and bioinformatic efforts. Hunter’s current work concentrates on integrating clinical observations with computational biology to discover new drug targets and to start the processes of bringing personalized medicine to patients with WM.

“Since the beginning, the IWMF has sought to raise awareness about Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia and find better treatments for this complex disease,” said IWMF Board Chair Paul Kitchen. “We are excited to support Dana-Farber’s innovative research, which aims to deepen our understanding of WM and pave the way for new treatment strategies and better outcomes for patients.”

jetpack-related-posts.title: IWMF awards $1.4 million to Dana-Farber investigators, fueling Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: For more than two decades, the International Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia Foundation (IWMF) has been a vital philanthropic partner to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, accelerating research into Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinemia (WM), a rare, slow-growing blood cancer.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Furthering research into new treatment for Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinemia
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: More than 10 years ago, Steven Treon, MD, PhD, and his colleagues were the first scientists to discover that MYD88 mutations, which occur in more than 95% of patients with Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia (WM), rely on the BTK protein to function.

jetpack-related-posts.title: New multi-institution network to drive progress in rare blood cancer
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The International Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia Foundation (IWMF) recently committed $2.5 million to support a new multi-institutional network for clinical and research programs dedicated to Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia (WM).

jetpack-related-posts.title: Luigi and Patrizia D’Amato
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Luigi and Patrizia D’Amato made a gift of $100,000 to support research within the Bing Center for Waldenström’s Macroglobulinemia at Dana-Farber. The center is the largest in the world dedicated to the study of Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia, a slow-growing type of blood cancer that most often forms in the bone marrow.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Fred and Michele Brettschneider
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Fred and Michele Brettschneider made a commitment of $250,000 to support a clinical trial network for Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia and advance all clinical research for this rare form of blood cancer within the Bing Center for Waldenström’s Macroglobulinemia.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Robert Cummins
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Robert Cummins gave $100,000 to establish The Deborah Cummins Waldenström’s Memorial Fund in honor of his late wife. Cummins’ investment is enabling a team at Dana-Farber’s Bing Center for Waldenström’s Macroglobulinemia to lead clinical trials that are pivotal in the development of more durable, effective treatments.

title.rendered: Bill Pomeroy gives the gift of access to patients with blood cancers

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Elyse Pleickhardt

In 2004, when William “Bill” Pomeroy was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a fast-growing blood and bone marrow cancer, his future was uncertain.

At that time, it was difficult for older adults with blood cancers to access stem cell transplants, despite the median age of diagnosis being 68. Transplants were typically reserved for those age 35 and younger, and even when an older patient did receive one, the risk of complications was much higher.

But in May 2005, Pomeroy got the fortunate news that a stem cell donor match had been found, and, before he knew it, he was on his way to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute for his transplant.

After his successful transplant, Pomeroy was inspired to help create better outcomes for patients like him. In 2005, he founded the William G. Pomeroy Foundation® to raise awareness and fund initiatives to improve access to blood cancer care. Pomeroy and his foundation have since made gifts totaling more than $1 million to Dana-Farber, supporting research and clinical trials that continue to make leaps and bounds toward more successful transplants.

“Over the past two decades, I have been proud to support Dana-Farber’s lifesaving mission through philanthropy,” said Pomeroy. “Giving back is my way of ensuring that others receive the same opportunity I was so fortunate to experience and to bring hope to patients facing some of life’s toughest challenges. None of us got to where we are on our own.”

Thanks to Pomeroy’s efforts, Dana-Farber has extended stem cell transplant treatment to people into their 70s and 80s and developed new ways of preparing people for transplants so they have better outcomes. Because access to treatment is so important to Pomeroy, one of his recent gifts supports the work of Coleman Lindsley, MD, PhD, whose Stem Cell Donor Registry Study has the potential to redefine how donors are selected for transplant and increase accessibility of this lifesaving treatment.

“This research paves the way for more effective and equitable treatment by exploring donor characteristics beyond age and antigen matching,” Pomeroy said. “Every gift, large or small, helps shape a healthier, brighter future for all.”

Pomeroy’s commitment is bringing blood cancer care to a population who, not so long ago, wasn’t eligible for lifesaving treatment. Dana-Farber and all the patients whose lives his generosity touches are forever grateful for the gift of access.

title.rendered: Gift from Haroun Family drives critical research for adult patients with Ewing sarcoma

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Caitlin Henault

When Rob Haroun was diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma, he knew where to go to find the most supportive and innovative care environment: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. After receiving treatment for leukemia years earlier at multiple health care centers, he and his family found that nothing compared to the care and attention he received at Dana-Farber.

“From the reception staff to the care teams, my experience at Dana-Farber has been head and shoulders above the rest,” said Rob. “It is clear that Dana- Farber is full of intelligent, responsive, and dedicated people.”

Grateful for his care team, led by Priscilla Merriam, MD, clinical director of the Sarcoma Center, and hoping to improve treatment options available to patients with Ewing sarcoma, Rob and his wife, Julie, established the Haroun Family Fund with a generous gift of $1 million. Under the leadership of Suzanne George, MD, chief of the Division of Sarcoma, the fund will support innovative research aimed at discovering the next breakthroughs in treating Ewing sarcoma in adults.

“It is clear that Dana-Farber is full of intelligent, responsive, and dedicated people.”

Rob Haroun

“Due to their rarity, sarcomas receive minimal support from external funding sources, slowing scientific progress and limiting treatments currently available to patients—especially adults who are diagnosed with cancers typically seen and studied in children,” said George. “Philanthropic support from visionary donors like the Harouns is critical to bringing better treatments to patients with these rare diseases.”

The first portion of the Haroun family’s gift will support the efforts of George Demetri, MD, senior vice president for Experimental Therapeutics and the Quick Family Chair in Medical Oncology at Dana-Farber, to test a promising new drug candidate that targets a protein unique to Ewing sarcoma. The second portion will fund innovative research initiatives focused on Ewing sarcoma—chosen through an internal grant proposal process—led by Francesca Alvarez Calderon, MD, PhD; Ryan Collins, PhD; Alan D’Andrea, MD, director of the Susan F. Smith Center for Women’s Cancers, director of the Center for DNA Damage and Repair; and Riaz Gillani, MD.

“Julie and I have been very blessed in our lives—I wouldn’t change anything even if it meant being disease free,” said Rob. “While a cure is the ultimate goal post that drives this gift, any research that slows the disease and puts it into remission would be transformational.”

Added Julie, “our commitment to this research is personal, but we find comfort in the fact that it will benefit so many patients who are facing Ewing sarcoma and other rare cancers.”

excerpt.rendered: Rob Haroun and his wife, Julie, established the Haroun Family Fund with a generous gift of $1 million. Under the leadership of Suzanne George, MD, chief of the Division of Sarcoma, the fund will support innovative research aimed at discovering the next breakthroughs in treating Ewing sarcoma in adults.

title.rendered: Donor bequeaths $1 million gift to metastatic breast cancer research

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Robbie Merritt

Through an estate provision added to her will, Anne P. Olsen has bequeathed $1 million to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. The gift will be directed to the Hilary J. Olsen Fund for Metastatic Breast Cancer, which was established in 2019 by Anne’s son, Jeff. The fund is in memory of Jeff’s late wife Hilary, who was treated twice for metastatic breast cancer (MBC) at Dana-Farber.

Anne’s generous gift, prompted by her daughter-in-law’s diagnosis as well as the diagnosis of her mother, sister, and grandmother all with breast cancer, will support the research of Erica L. Mayer, MD, MPH, director of breast cancer clinical research at Dana-Farber. Mayer cared for Hilary from the time of her breast cancer recurrence in 2015 until her passing in November 2018.

“Cancer is a disease that has affected my whole family, so it feels good to give back,” Anne said. “With metastatic cancers especially, funding for research and testing is so important to be able to understand the unique profile of each patient’s cancer and select the best therapies for them.”

“You hear more stories today than ever before of people surviving for years with metastatic cancers, so it’s a hopeful area, but it has a long way to go,” added Anne’s son, Jeff. “You can see changes in results every day, and it’s important to continue that momentum.”
Through the Olsen Fund, Anne’s bequest will bolster critical care and research for MBC patients at Dana-Farber, including clinical trials and fellowship opportunities, and support Mayer’s research on understanding tumor biology and investigating novel targeted therapies that may shape the future of breast cancer care.

“Not only am I grateful for these funds, which will help drive forward critical work in the breast cancer space, but I am also so heartened that this fund will continue to keep Hilary’s legacy alive,” said Mayer. “Hilary was such a special person, with enormous kindness, enthusiasm, humor, and an incredible ability to support everyone around her. I was so honored to care for her and to meet her amazing family.”

As part of her $1 million bequest, Anne has committed to making annual gifts to the Olsen Fund through her son Jeff’s participation in the Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), the sum of which will be credited toward her bequest. Jeff rides in the PMC as captain of Team Bunger’s Bikers and directs his fundraising to the Olsen Fund. He has participated in the annual two-day bike-a-thon since 2008.

title.rendered: Prostate Cancer Foundation fuels Dana-Farber innovation with $1M+ in grants

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Casey Reis

For more than 30 years, the Prostate Cancer Foundation (PCF) has been at the forefront of prostate cancer research, funding revolutionary studies and fostering collaboration among physician-scientists. PCF recently awarded $1,050,000 to three Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers through two Young Investigator Awards and one Challenge Award, each supporting research projects aimed at combating prostate cancer and improving outcomes for patients. The grants underscore PCF’s longstanding commitment to advancing transformational research and nurturing the next generation of leaders in the field.

Sylvan Baca, MD, PhD, is the recipient of the 2024 American Cancer Society-PCF Young Investigator Award, a grant designed to support promising early career scientists who are poised to make notable achievements in prostate cancer research. Baca’s team developed a novel platform for liquid biopsies—or blood tests that evaluate cancer on a molecular level rather than with invasive tumor biopsies—monitoring changes in cancer from patient plasma. If successful, the project will assist in disease monitoring, the evaluation of treatment response, and guiding therapy.

Martin Bakht, PhD, has been honored with the 2024 Michael and Lori Milken Family Foundation-PCF Young Investigator Award to support research on metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and mechanisms of resistance to the targeted therapy currently used for treatment. The goal is to gain new insights that will lead to developing strategies for overcoming resistance and improving patient outcomes.

A cross-disciplinary team led by Alan D’Andrea, MD, has received a 2024 PCF Challenge Award for work aiming to refine combination therapies, inhibiting certain pathways to prevent cancer cells from repairing their DNA. D’Andrea’s lab is studying new uses for a drug called novobiocin (NVB) and is collaborating with the National Cancer Institute to test NVB in clinical trials, testing it on its own and in combination with other drugs to evaluate its efficacy and expand upon the understanding and treatment of prostate cancer.

PCF’s generosity not only supports cutting-edge research but also reinforces its dedication to advancing innovation.

“We are honored to support the talented physician-scientists at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute by investing in these promising projects,” said PCF President and CEO Gina B. Carithers. “Together, the PCF and Dana-Farber are paving the way for breakthroughs that could transform the landscape of prostate cancer treatment and improve outcomes for patients worldwide.”

jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Prostate Cancer Foundation has awarded $1.45 million in grants to three Dana-Farber investigators researching more powerful treatments for the disease.

jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Prostate Cancer Foundation (PCF) has awarded grants totaling more than $2.3 million to Dana-Farber researchers.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Prostate Cancer Research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Prostate Cancer Research gave nearly $400,000 in support of a Dana-Farber study that aims to improve prostate cancer screening equity. title.rendered: The Kesslers’ vision for advancing AML research

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Lucy McDonald

Distinguished Trustee Michele Kessler and her husband Howard have long stood as pillars of innovation and philanthropy, consistently championing medical research and initiatives that drive advancements in cancer care. Their commitment to these causes is rooted in a profound belief in the power of collaboration. “In my opinion, I think there is a cure. If everyone collaborated like the Manhattan Project, in two or three years, we could solve it. We need people to have that same intention,” Howard said, reflecting on his unwavering belief in a collective effort to defy cancer. A visionary in both business and civic spheres, Howard is no stranger to transformative endeavors.

The Kesslers have been steadfast leaders in Dana-Farber’s philanthropic community. Michele, who became a Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Trustee in 2000, has consistently supported the Institute’s mission through her leadership of various events and campaigns. Their relationship with Dana-Farber deepened when Howard began receiving treatment for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This personal connection has only strengthened their commitment to support cancer research and treatment.

Howard’s approach to tackling complex and challenging causes is marked by determination and a straightforward, guiding principle: “I want to make a difference by creating alternative solutions,” he said of his goal. “Helping people realize what we can do to overcome cancer.” His passion for finding solutions for people with cancer is matched only by his admiration for his wife of 55 years, Michele. “She gave me confidence. She made all the difference in my life,” he shared, highlighting the personal support that fuels his philanthropic spirit.

In a recent demonstration of their enduring generosity, the Kesslers donated $1 million to advance AML research led by Robert Soiffer, MD, chief of the Division of Hematologic Malignancies and Worthington and Margaret Collette Professor of Medicine in the Field of Hematologic Oncology at Harvard Medical School. This substantial gift will empower Soiffer and his team to continue their vital work pursuing personalized approaches to optimize donor cell efficiency, which is crucial in AML treatment. With this funding, Soiffer is poised to leverage findings from previous clinical trials and investigate how new techniques could be applied to AML treatment. Together, these methods represent the most comprehensive approach to enhance transplant success and improve patient outcomes.

This gift embodies a shared vision between Soiffer and the Kesslers: working together leads to innovative solutions. The support not only enhances the potential for groundbreaking discoveries but also reinforces the importance of fostering collaboration to provide a rich foundation for future research. As a result, the future of AML treatment looks brighter, offering renewed hope to patients and families around the world.

title.rendered: The Donahues drive research into liquid biopsy for early detection and personalized medicine

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Michael Quinn

Team science fueled by philanthropy has always provided a driving force for Dana-Farber’s progress against cancer. As loyal Institute supporters, Digger and Susan Donahue play an integral role in this team effort and continually step forward to elevate it.

Recently, Digger and Susan made a generous gift of $1 million to the Donahue Family Fund for Prostate Cancer and the Donahue Family Fund for Cancer Interception at Dana-Farber. Their gift accelerates research to advance a novel liquid biopsy led by Toni Choueiri, MD, director of Dana-Farber’s Lank Center for Genitourinary Oncology and the Jerome and Nancy Kohlberg Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School; and Matthew Freedman, MD, the David Goldstein Chair at Dana-Farber.

Launched with the help of the Donahues’ initial gift to the project in 2020, this first-of-its-kind biopsy leverages the power of epigenetics to uncover tumor biology and ultimately inform treatment decisions. While genetic changes involve variations to the DNA sequence itself, epigenetic changes affect which genes are “expressed”—meaning turned on or off like a light switch—including genes implicated in cancer development and therapeutic resistance. By analyzing tumor-derived DNA fragments in the blood and urine to detect these chemical changes, the biopsy determines what type of cancer a patient has, which therapies the disease might respond to, and whether it is resistant to a particular drug. As a result, the test advances personalized cancer medicine that maximizes efficacy and minimizes side effects. Additionally, the liquid biopsy has the future aim of increasing patient access to potentially lifesaving early detection by providing an upgraded procedure that is less expensive, time-intensive, and invasive than a physical tissue biopsy.

With the Donahues’ sustained investment, Institute investigators were able to enhance and expand the biopsy, which was initially focused on prostate cancer, to address 14 different malignancies, including bladder, colon, lung, and skin cancers. According to Choueiri, such progress demonstrates the importance of the Donahues’ encouragement and impact of their philanthropy. “It means so much to count on Digger’s and Susan’s continued partnership,” he said. “Because of them, our multidisciplinary team can improve this test and bring it to clinics more quickly so it benefits patients everywhere.”

The Donahues are committed to supporting Dana-Farber’s team because they believe in the potential impact of the liquid biopsy. “A less invasive biopsy technique represents a real game-changer,” said Digger. “This test will provide an exciting opportunity for earlier diagnoses of cancers to save more lives,” Susan said. “We’re pleased to see so much progress and glad to be a part of it.”

jetpack-related-posts.title: Advancing early detection research through the Larry and Susan Marx Fund
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Larry and Susan Marx established the Larry and Susan Marx Fund for Early Detection with a $2.6 million gift, supporting efforts to detect and screen cancers earlier and improve treatment outcomes.

img.alt_text: Susan and Larry Marx in biking gear

jetpack-related-posts.title: Craig and Bettina Burr
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Craig and Bettina Burr gave $100,000 towards the Bettina and Craig Burr Breast Cancer Genetics and Prevention Research Fund at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. This gift will support the research of Judy Garber, MD, MPH, the Susan F. Smith Chair at Dana-Farber, and Myles Brown, MD, the Emil Frei III, MD,…

jetpack-related-posts.title: Prevention is goal of groundbreaking immunotherapy trial
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: When asked what motivates her to support cancer research, Susan Hertog starts at the beginning, when her best friend was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer at the age of 49.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Stanley and Carol Riemer
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Carol and Stanley Riemer’s most recent commitment has established the Riemer Family Fund for Pancreatic Cancer Early Detection at Dana-Farber, in honor of late relatives who developed pancreatic cancer. Under the leadership of Matthew Yurgelun, MD, their support aims to develop groundbreaking early detection blood tests for high-risk patients.

jetpack-related-posts.title: William and Barbara Connolly
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s Sara M. Tolaney, MD, MPH, received a $100,000 gift from the Connolly Family Fund, established by William and Barbara Connolly, to advance innovative breast cancer research. Their support empowers Tolaney’s team to develop novel strategies for early detection, prevention, and personalized treatment, helping to improve outcomes for…

jetpack-related-posts.title: Susan G. Komen strengthens commitment to breast cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: In 2024, Komen reaffirmed its dedication to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute by awarding three new Career Transition Awards totaling $1.95 million, alongside 12 active research grants. This investment underscores Komen's ongoing support for groundbreaking studies and improving outcomes for those affected by breast cancer.

title.rendered: BRCA gene mutations are focus of $1 million research fund

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Kathy Clute

Between them, Wayland resident Donna Hale and her sister Nancy have been successfully treated for cancer five times. They were more susceptible to the disease because of a mutation in one of their BRCA genes. Mutations in BRCA1 and/or BRCA2 increase the risk of developing certain cancers, particularly of the breast, ovaries, pancreas, and prostate.

When Donna’s breast cancer was first discovered in 1999, routine testing for mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes was not common. But after Nancy got breast cancer five years later and then was diagnosed with lung cancer in 2019, she underwent testing that revealed the genetic vulnerability. Donna immediately got genetic testing as well.

“I tell my sister that she really saved my life,” said Donna, a longtime Dana-Farber supporter along with her husband, John Donovan. “If she hadn’t had lung cancer, I would not have been tested, and they wouldn’t have found my ovarian cancer.” That cancer was discovered only when she underwent preventative surgery to remove her reproductive organs in 2020.

In gratitude for the care Donna received at Dana-Farber and concerned about possible cuts to the Institute’s federal research funding, she and John donated $1 million earlier this year to establish a research fund in support of The Mellen and Eisenson Family Center for BRCA and Related Genes. It will be managed by Judy Garber, MD, MPH, Susan F. Smith Chair and chief of the Division of Cancer Genetics and Prevention. Garber has been Donna’s breast oncologist.

The money will help revolutionize the treatment of BRCA-driven cancers by supporting three key priorities: development of a blood test to identify ovarian cancer via circulating microRNA (small pieces of genetic material) before symptoms appear; clinical trials of better, more precise treatments for patients with BRCA-related tumors; and research into how to reduce breast cancer risk in women taking hormones to offset menopause symptoms after prophylactic ovary removal.

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes that help repair breaks in DNA, a process that is essential to prevent cells from growing and dividing uncontrollably and forming into tumors. Genetic testing is recommended for individuals with a known history of BRCA-driven tumors, but more than half of all people with BRCA mutations have no family history of cancer. Ovarian cancer, for example, is typically not diagnosed until a late stage because there are no screening tests and early symptoms can easily be mistaken for common conditions.

“BRCA is emblazoned on our frontal lobes because of Donna, Nancy, and our two daughters, so we wanted to support research that would benefit people with the mutations,” said John. “The science is so important, and we were anxious to help fund it.”

It will be managed by Judy Garber, MD, MPH, Susan F. Smith Chair and chief of the Division of Cancer Genetics and Prevention. Garber has been Donna’s breast oncologist.

jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Philanthropy has transformative power to address society’s intractable challenges. The Gray Foundation is committed to this goal and, with two grants totaling nearly $6 million, is harnessing this power for good through The Dana-Farber Campaign.

jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty

jetpack-related-posts.title: Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation gift focuses on cancer interception
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: A $1.25 million gift to Dana-Farber from the Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation supports research focused on ways pancreatic cancer might be detected—and intercepted—before it can be seen on CT scans or other imaging modalities.

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Tarice Gray

In June, Dana-Farber received the key regulatory approvals needed to advance our plans to build New England’s only dedicated inpatient cancer hospital for adult patients. Owned and operated by Dana-Farber, the Future Cancer Hospital will be an independent cancer facility. A new Dana-Farber cancer hospital—combined with our transformational future clinical collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, a Harvard affiliated academic medical center, and its physician group, Harvard Medical Faculty Physicians—will deliver fully integrated, world-class cancer care in a setting devoted exclusively to healing and hope. It is the right care model for the future of cancer care and will allow us to provide the best care for our patients for years to come. A visionary new facility that will redefine how cancer is treated, the Future Cancer Hospital will offer 450,000 square feet of dedicated patient care space, 300 private inpatient beds—including 30 licensed ICU beds and 16-bed observation suite, and specialized facilities.

Bringing this innovative care model to life depends, in part, on visionary philanthropy. The partnership of our dedicated community of benefactors will make this bold and ambitious vision for the future of cancer care a reality—creating a world where all patients receive integrated, best-in-class inpatient and outpatient care from an exceptional team of clinicians and scientists focused solely on cancer. Please visit www.dana-farber.org/about/our-vision-for-the-future-of-cancer-care for more information.

title.rendered: AACR grants support sarcoma, renal cell carcinoma, and cancer biology research

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Cyrena Musset

The American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) recently awarded $580,000 to three Dana-Farber physician-scientists who are investigating new methods of prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of various types of cancers. As the first cancer research organization dedicated to preventing and curing cancer, AACR is a long-standing partner in Dana-Farber’s mission to defy cancer.

Erica Pimenta, MD, PhD, Medical Oncology Fellow, is clinically and scientifically focused on sarcoma, which develops in bone and connective tissue. Her work involves studying pathogenesis and immune evasion, leveraging both computational and molecular biology approaches.

“I am extremely grateful and honored to be awarded the AACR-QuadW Foundation Sarcoma Research Fellowship in Memory of Willie Tichenor,” said Pimenta. “As a sarcoma-focused physician-scientist, I can assure patients that sarcoma research is active and advanced. This award supports the continuation of vital work, providing protected research time for excellence in biologic discovery. Thank you to all who made this possible.”

Cary Weiss, MD, PhD, Pediatric Hematology/Oncology Fellow, studies translocation renal cell carcinoma, a rare and aggressive type of kidney cancer that is more common in children, young people, women, and as a secondary malignancy. He’s working on a new approach using Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras, which are special molecules designed to break down harmful proteins quickly and completely.

“I am thrilled to be awarded the AACR-Exelixis Renal Cell Carcinoma Research Fellowship, which provides essential funding to advance my research on translocation renal cell carcinoma and supports my development as an independent physician-scientist,” said Weiss. “This opportunity significantly contributes to my goal of improving outcomes for pediatric and adolescent/young adult cancer patients.”

Dana-Farber researcher, Nika Danial, PhD, in collaboration with Jarrod Marto, PhD and Mariella Filbin, MD, PhD, are researching histone mutant diffuse midline gliomas, a type of brain tumor caused by certain cells that should develop into glial cells but instead stay in an immature “stem-like” state.

“This award will catalyze high-risk, high-reward studies that could lead to significant breakthroughs in understanding how certain lipid-protein interactions affect glioma, an untapped area of discovery in metabolic signaling,” said Danial. “The findings could also impact our understanding of other cancers where cell development is disrupted or stalled.”

jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation has awarded $1.22 million in grants to four early career investigators at Dana-Farber whose research has the potential to yield important breakthroughs in cancer prevention, diagnosis, and treatment.

jetpack-related-posts.title: IMS grants drive innovative multiple myeloma research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The International Myeloma Society (IMS) recently awarded three Dana-Farber scientists grants totaling $525,000 to promote research on the blood cancer multiple myeloma.

jetpack-related-posts.title: American Cancer Society grants propel research and programs forward
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The American Cancer Society (ACS) recently awarded more than $3.1 million in grants to 11 Dana-Farber Cancer Institute investigators. These grants support various areas across Dana-Farber, including research on improved outcomes and patient assistance programming to help with access to care.

title.rendered: Cookies for Kids’ Cancer funds groundbreaking Dana-Farber pediatric cancer research

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

Cookies for Kids’ Cancer has awarded two grants totaling $600,000 to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to support groundbreaking pediatric cancer research. The funding supports two projects: one led by A. Thomas Look, MD, focused on high-risk neuroblastoma, and another led by Scott Armstrong, MD, PhD, targeting a rare and aggressive form of childhood leukemia. This is part of their ongoing commitment, having previously funded more than $2.6 million in pediatric cancer research grants to Dana-Farber through a rigorous peer-reviewed process.

Look received a $300,000 grant in 2025 to advance treatments for children with high-risk neuroblastoma. These patients often endure a year of intensive treatment followed by post-consolidation therapy, which includes isotretinoin and an anti-GD2 antibody. While this regimen improves survival, many children relapse due to treatment limitations. Look’s research arose from a screen that identified a drug, PF-9363, which works synergistically with isotretinoin to extend suppression of cancer cell growth and increase the expression of GD2, making neuroblastoma cells more vulnerable to immunotherapy that specifically targets this cell surface glycolipid. This combination therapy significantly improved the killing of human neuroblastoma cells growing in immunosuppressed mice and was well tolerated. His team is now testing a three-drug regimen—including PF-9363, isotretinoin, and the anti-GD2 antibody—in this model system to validate a treatment schedule suitable for testing to improve outcomes for children with neuroblastoma. If successful, this could lead to clinical trials and offer new hope for children with treatment-resistant neuroblastoma.

“There’s a critical need to develop smarter, more targeted treatments for these children,” Armstrong said. “Our goal is to bring therapies to the clinic that directly address the biology of their disease and improve their chances of survival.”

Scott Armstrong, MD, PhD, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute

Cookies for Kids’ Cancer awarded Armstrong a $300,000 grant in 2024 to study childhood leukemia with NUP98 gene rearrangements, which are associated with poor outcomes and limited treatment options. His team is targeting the Menin-KMT2A complex, a key driver of leukemia gene expression, and exploring a second target, KAT6A, for combination therapy.

“There’s a critical need to develop smarter, more targeted treatments for these children,” Armstrong said. “Our goal is to bring therapies to the clinic that directly address the biology of their disease and improve their chances of survival.”

Thanks to funding from Cookies for Kids’ Cancer and the revolutionary work of two Dana-Farber researchers, these studies represent a significant step toward better outcomes for children with some of the most challenging pediatric cancers.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Grants support innovations in pediatric cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: For over 12 years, grants awarded by Hyundai Hope On Wheels® totaling over $5.5 million have supported Dana-Farber investigators and their research to further discovery, leverage new technologies, and revolutionize treatment for pediatric patients everywhere.

jetpack-related-posts.title: METAvivor advances metastatic breast cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: METAvivor has awarded three grants totaling $850,000 to advance metastatic breast cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Anne Marie & Salvatore Torregrossa
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Anne Marie and Salvatore Torregrossa made a generous $100,000 gift to support pediatric cancer research and care led by Lisa Diller, MD, at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Their contribution will help advance groundbreaking discoveries and improve care for children facing cancer, continuing Torregrossa’s legacy of compassion and commitment to our lifesaving…

jetpack-related-posts.title: CLL Global Research Foundation
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The CLL Global Research Foundation awarded generous grants totaling $600,000 to Dana-Farber, supporting the research of Catherine Wu, MD, Lavine Family Chair for Preventative Cancer Therapies, and Erin Parry, MD, PhD. This funding will help advance their studies of chronic lymphocytic leukemia, aiming to uncover new insights and improve treatment…

jetpack-related-posts.title: Rally Foundation supports bold pediatric cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Rally Foundation for Childhood Cancer Research recently awarded $450,000 in grants to four Dana-Farber researchers developing innovative treatments for pediatric cancer.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Stop & Shop raises over $760,000 for pediatric cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: This spring, New England Stop & Shop customers donated over $760,000 to pediatric cancer research at Dana-Farber through the grocery chain’s annual Help Cure Childhood Cancer campaign.

title.rendered: Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation helps advance glioblastoma research

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

The Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation has awarded $524,081 to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to advance novel immunotherapy approaches to treat glioblastoma. This funding supports a project focused on a novel treatment strategy for glioblastoma led by David Reardon, MD, Clinical Director of the Center for Neuro-Oncology and Alperin Family Chair in Neuro-Oncology at Dana-Farber.

Glioblastoma is an aggressive brain cancer with limited treatment options and a median survival of just 15 months. Most patients experience tumor recurrence, and few therapies offer meaningful benefit after relapse. Unlike other cancers that respond well to immunotherapy, glioblastoma has proven resistant due to its “cold” tumor environment. This “cold” tumor environment lacks immune cell activity and actively suppresses immune responses.

CUE-102, an investigational drug, aims to overcome this barrier. It is designed to activate and expand the body’s own cancer-fighting T cells that target a protein called Wilms Tumor 1 (WT1), which is expressed in nearly all glioblastomas. Because it works in the bloodstream and lymph nodes—rather than needing to cross into the brain—CUE-102 primes the immune system to recognize and destroy tumor cells.

“Glioblastoma has long resisted the kinds of immune-based treatments that have transformed care for other cancers,” said Reardon. “CUE-102 represents a novel strategy to awaken the immune system and direct it against a target commonly found in these tumors.”

Early clinical trial results with CUE-102 for other cancers are promising: the treatment appears safe, with mostly mild side effects, and nearly half of all patients experienced disease control. Importantly, the study confirmed that CUE-102 successfully activated the targeted immune cells.

“Glioblastoma has long resisted the kinds of immune-based treatments that have transformed care for other cancers,” said Reardon. “CUE-102 represents a novel strategy to awaken the immune system and direct it against a target commonly found in these tumors.”

David Reardon, MD, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute

This work represents a critical step forward in addressing one of the most challenging cancers. It is made possible through the generous support of the Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation, whose dedication to cancer research is helping to drive innovation and hope.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Massachusetts Life Sciences Center fuels advances in immunotherapy and workforce development
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute has received nearly $800,000 in support from the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center (MLSC) to advance cancer research and workforce development.

jetpack-related-posts.title: CLL Global Research Foundation
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The CLL Global Research Foundation awarded generous grants totaling $600,000 to Dana-Farber, supporting the research of Catherine Wu, MD, Lavine Family Chair for Preventative Cancer Therapies, and Erin Parry, MD, PhD. This funding will help advance their studies of chronic lymphocytic leukemia, aiming to uncover new insights and improve treatment…

jetpack-related-posts.title: The DeGregorio Family Foundation continues to advance gastroesophageal cancer treatment
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Gastric and esophageal cancers often resist chemotherapy and metastasize easily. The DeGregorio Family Foundation aims to address this challenge with more than $500,000 in grant funding to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to develop new treatments.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Cookies for Kids’ Cancer funds groundbreaking Dana-Farber pediatric cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Cookies for Kids’ Cancer has awarded two grants totaling $600,000 to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to support groundbreaking pediatric cancer research.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Dana-Farber Campaign: The promise of personalized cancer vaccines
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Funds raised through The Dana-Farber campaign are expanding the benefits of personalized cancer vaccines pioneered here.

img.alt_text: Two scientists examining a slide in a lab

jetpack-related-posts.title: 3000 Miles to a Cure
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: 3000 Miles to a Cure awarded $100,000 to support the ALLELE-GBM research program at Dana-Farber, under the direction of Keith Ligon, MD, PhD. Ligon’s team is working to put genomic data into the hands of patients, providers, and researchers to advance treatments and clinical trials in glioblastoma (GBM).

title.rendered: METAvivor advances metastatic breast cancer research

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

METAvivor has awarded three grants totaling $850,000 to advance metastatic breast cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. More than half of this funding—$450,000—supports a project led by Rinath Jeselsohn, MD, which aims to develop a clinically accessible tool to help physicians predict which patients with advanced hormone receptor-positive breast cancer will respond to a common treatment combination. By analyzing routine clinical and tumor data, the tool—based on a machine learning algorithm—aims to guide more personalized treatment choices and reduce exposure to less effective therapies. The study will also explore how the immune environment of tumors may contribute to treatment resistance.

The remaining two grants of $200,000 each support early career investigators Stefania Morganti, MD, and Paolo Tarantino, MD, PhD. Morganti is investing the role of minimal residual disease via circulating tumor DNA in patients with HER2+ metastatic breast cancer (MBC) and exceptional response to therapy. Tarantino’s research focuses on innovating and refining methods to predict responses to antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) therapies in patients with advanced breast cancer. Tarantino said, “Antibody-Drug Conjugates have had a transformative impact on the prognosis of MBC, but we’re still unable to adequately tailor their use. With the critical support of METAvivor, we plan to leverage cutting-edge technologies to learn from our patients’ samples and develop biomarkers for precision ADC treatment”

Kelly Shanahan, MD, President of METAvivor, emphasizes the organization’s commitment. She said, “METAvivor funds the best in research focused on people whose breast cancer has already metastasized, which is why nine Dana-Farber investigators have been awarded METAvivor research awards since 2019, more than any other institution. As someone living with MBC, I am grateful for the brilliant minds at Dana Farber who are developing treatments that will help me and people like me live longer and better.”

“METAvivor funds the best in research focused on people whose breast cancer has already metastasized, which is why nine Dana-Farber investigators have been awarded METAvivor research awards since 2019, more than any other institution. As someone living with MBC, I am grateful for the brilliant minds at Dana Farber who are developing treatments that will help me and people like me live longer and better.”

Kelly Shanahan, MD, President of METAvivor

Through these grants, METAvivor continues to make a significant impact on MBC, fostering advancements that promise to improve patient outcomes and extend lives.

title.rendered: Massachusetts Life Sciences Center fuels advances in immunotherapy and workforce development

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

Dana-Farber Cancer Institute has received nearly $800,000 in support from the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center (MLSC) to advance cancer research and workforce development. This funding supports two pivotal initiatives focused on access and equity: the Continuing Umbrella Research Experiences (CURE) Program and a groundbreaking project in novel therapeutics delivery.

Eric Smith, MD, PhD received a $750,000 grant for his work in novel therapeutics delivery. Working in partnership with Massachusetts clinical-stage biotechnology company, Strand Therapeutics, the team, which includes a postdoc hired specifically for this project, has been working together to optimize an RNA approach for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) delivery in patients, aiming to transform cancer immunotherapy. Such an approach could circumvent the resource-intensive manufacturing processes deployed in current CAR therapies, thereby making advanced CAR therapies more accessible to underserved populations and patients with rare cancers. The project promises to enhance accessibility, speed, and efficacy of treatment, offering hope to those who lack access to tertiary care centers.

Kirk Taylor, MD, President and CEO of MLSC, said, “If successful, this project will revolutionize cancer treatment accessibility, offering rapid and cost-effective solutions to patients in need. We are proud to support Dana-Farber’s innovative work that aligns with our mission to advance life sciences and improve patient outcomes.”

The MLSC Novel Therapeutics Delivery program fosters collaboration across engineering, biology, chemistry, and medicine, addressing complex challenges in therapeutic delivery. With this funding, Dana-Farber is poised to make significant strides in cancer research, offering hope to patients and communities worldwide.

“If successful, this project will revolutionize cancer treatment accessibility, offering rapid and cost-effective solutions to patients in need. We are proud to support Dana-Farber’s innovative work that aligns with our mission to advance life sciences and improve patient outcomes.”

Kirk Taylor, MD, President and CEO of MLSC

Karen Burns White, deputy associate director of Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center Community Engagement and Outreach, received more than $43,000 for the 2024 CURE Program. This initiative provides student intern stipends, fostering the next generation of researchers committed to health equity and reducing the inequitable burden of cancer. Burns White emphasizes the importance of early exposure and engagement to all levels of cancer research and care. MLSC has been a dedicated partner to the CURE Program, broadening opportunities for students across Massachusetts and helping to ensure a future healthcare workforce of well-prepared, highly skilled, and diverse candidates. The MLSC has provided over $130,000 to support a total of 37 internships since 2018.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Investment in infrastructure accelerates immunotherapy development
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Massachusetts Life Sciences Center (MLSC) has granted Dana-Farber $2.78 million to build crucial infrastructure for developing immunotherapies—novel treatments that leverage the immune system to fight cancer.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Massachusetts Life Sciences Center grants $2.8 million to establish new center and accelerate drug development
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Massachusetts Life Sciences Center (MLSC) has awarded Dana-Farber $2,811,397 to establish a Center for Emergent Drug Targets (CEDT), which will provide a collaborative environment to streamline and accelerate the earliest stages of drug discovery.

img.alt_text: Sara Buhrlage, PhD, and Jarrod Marto, PhD

jetpack-related-posts.title: Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation helps advance glioblastoma research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation has awarded $524,081 to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to advance novel immunotherapy approaches to treat glioblastoma.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Cookies for Kids’ Cancer funds groundbreaking Dana-Farber pediatric cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Cookies for Kids’ Cancer has awarded two grants totaling $600,000 to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to support groundbreaking pediatric cancer research.

jetpack-related-posts.title: METAvivor advances metastatic breast cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: METAvivor has awarded three grants totaling $850,000 to advance metastatic breast cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

jetpack-related-posts.title: TA Associates
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: TA Associates made a generous, unrestricted gift of $170,000 to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Their vital support empowers the Institute to advance cancer research and patient care, fostering innovation and expanding access to treatment. TA's flexible commitment plays a crucial role in driving progress and improving outcomes for patients and families.

title.rendered: Rally Foundation supports bold pediatric cancer research

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

Rally Foundation for Childhood Cancer Research recently awarded $450,000 in grants to four Dana-Farber researchers developing innovative treatments for pediatric cancer. Recipients include Tom Rosenberg, MD; James Morrow, MD, PhD; Basudev Chowdhury, PhD; and Yana Pikman, MD.

Rosenberg is designing new therapies for children with recurrent atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor (ATRT), a rare and aggressive brain cancer that primarily affects infants. While current treatments cure nearly half of patients with ATRT, there are no effective therapies for patients whose disease recurs. In addition, the intensive therapy patients receive often causes significant long-term side effects. Rosenberg designed a platform study that will test safer, more targeted therapies.

Morrow is studying osteosarcoma, a bone cancer common in adolescents and young adults. Recent work has identified two tumor subtypes—one that resembles normal bone and responds well to treatment and another that behaves more like stem cells and spreads aggressively. Morrow is testing whether the latter can be reprogrammed into bone-like cells to improve outcomes. “Understanding what makes these tumors more aggressive may open the door to entirely new treatment strategies,” said Morrow.

Chowdhury is investigating the biology of pediatric leukemias, including acute lymphoblastic leukemia and acute myeloid leukemia. By studying molecular vulnerabilities in these cancers, his research could uncover new targets for treatment and lead to breakthrough therapies.

“Understanding what makes these tumors more aggressive could open the door to entirely new treatment strategies.”

James Morrow, MD, PhD

Pikman led the first national precision medicine trial using genomic testing to guide treatment for children with high-risk, relapsed, or treatment-resistant leukemia. She is now expanding this work to pediatric centers across the Northeast to assess how genomic testing impacts diagnosis and treatment of pediatric leukemia and testing the feasibility of offering extended genomic testing at the regional level. Her research seeks to improve access to testing, support clinicians in using genomic data, and ultimately reduce toxicity of treatment while improving survival.

These early stage, high potential studies represent Rally Foundation’s commitment to funding research that improves both outcomes and quality of life for children with cancer.

jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact

title.rendered: Inspiring hope: Catherine’s journey and the impact of Giving Day

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund’s annual Giving Day, held on Wednesday, May 21 this year, united patients, families, employees, and supporters worldwide in giving to Dana-Farber’s mission to defy cancer. All donations supporting Giving Day were tripled-matched to fuel groundbreaking research and compassionate care, thanks to a generous $250,000 gift from an anonymous Dana-Farber Trustee. During this Giving Day, over $832,000 was raised, surpassing the goal of $500,000 in unrestricted funds, with 94% of the total being unrestricted. This funding is crucial as it provides researchers the flexibility to pursue innovative treatments and breakthroughs at a rapid pace. Patients like Catherine benefit directly from the lifesaving research and care made possible through Giving Day.

Catherine’s journey with cancer began unexpectedly while living abroad in Geneva, Switzerland. At 30 weeks pregnant, she discovered a lump on her chest, initially dismissing it as a pregnancy-related issue. Her diagnosis of stage II triple-negative breast cancer came as a shock.

Faced with the daunting reality of cancer during pregnancy, Catherine found hope at Dana-Farber. “When I found out that Dana-Farber has a program specifically for patients diagnosed with cancer while pregnant, I felt a sense of relief,” she said. Under the care of Ann Partridge, MD, MPH, the Eric P. Winer, MD, Chair in Breast Cancer Research at Dana-Farber, Catherine embarked on a comprehensive treatment plan. “The care I have received at Dana-Farber has been nothing short of amazing,” she shared. Today, Catherine is grateful to Dana-Farber for the support that allows her to focus on her health and her family, including her newborn daughter, Camila, who was delivered safely and is perfectly healthy.

The success of Giving Day is a testament to the power of community. With the community’s support on Giving Day and every day, Dana-Farber maintains its momentum, ensuring we are there for every patient who walks through our doors.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Cancer Prevention Initiative
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Cancer Prevention Initiative (CPI) awarded $450,000 to Kornelia Polyak, MD, PhD, for her breast cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, targeting early tumor progression. This grant highlights CPI’s vital support for and shared mission with Dana-Farber in advancing impactful strategies for early medical interception of inherited cancer to improve…

jetpack-related-posts.title: Together in action, together in progress: Giving Day surpasses fundraising goal
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: This year’s annual Giving Day marked an especially generous occasion for dedicated supporters of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Phyllis and Richard Krock
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Institute Trustee Phyllis Krock and her husband, Richard, gave a generous gift of $100,000 to the Palm Beach Initiative. The funds are dedicated to the Presidential Initiatives Fund under Dana-Farber President and CEO Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD. With this support, Dana-Farber physicians and researchers can continue developing innovative cancer…

jetpack-related-posts.title: National Marrow Donor Program
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The NMDP provided a $400,000 grant to support the research of Nicoletta Cieri, MD, PhD, at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. This funding will support her work to improve allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation by identifying genetic factors influencing graft-versus-host disease, potentially leading to more personalized treatment strategies and improved patient outcomes.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Estate of Carolyn Brophy
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Estate of Carolyn Brophy has generously bequeathed $120,697.36 to support cancer research and care at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Carolyn’s commitment to Dana-Farber’s mission will drive promising research and innovative treatments. Her legacy will inspire breakthroughs and improve patient experiences, helping Dana-Farber continue to defy cancer.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Dana-Farber Society
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Dana-Farber Society (DFS) is a group of visionary donors who are changing lives and creating a legacy through a planned gift such as a bequest, life income gift, or beneficiary designation to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, the Jimmy Fund, the Friends of Dana-Farber, or the Pan-Mass Challenge.

title.rendered: Honoring whole blood and platelet donors

content.rendered:
Fall 2025
By Lori Dougherty
Photography by John Deputy

As much as any drug or technology, whole blood and platelets are lifesaving resources for cancer patients. The Kraft Family Blood Donor Center celebrates the compassionate individuals who give so generously at the center’s annual Breakfast of Champions. Sunday, Apr. 6 marked the 41st anniversary of the Kraft Family Blood Donor Center. Institute Trustee Dan Kraft welcomed 225 whole blood and platelet donors and guests to Gillette Stadium to celebrate 5,053 units of platelets, 7,516 units of whole blood, and 480 stem cell products they donated in the prior year. The donations made a powerful difference in the lives of 14,317 patients and their families.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Celebrating 40th anniversary of Kraft Family Blood Donor Center
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Whole blood and platelet donors were the stars at Gillette Stadium for the annual Kraft Family Blood Donor Center Breakfast of Champions. This year’s event marked the 40th anniversary of the Kraft Center.
